Introduction

Kinds of lists

Compare singly, doubly, and circularly linked lists.

Cost analysis

Evaluate the time and space costs of linked-list operations.

Basics

Kinds of Linked Lists

Singly linkedEach node points only to the next one; the last node points to null.
Doubly linkedEach node points to both the previous and the next node, so we can walk either way.
Circularly linkedThe last node points back to the first instead of null, closing the list into a ring.

In all three, items live not in adjacent cells, as in an array, but in nodes that point to one another.

Basics

Singly Linked List

  • Items are connected by one-way links: each item holds a reference to the one after it.
  • The list keeps a special reference to the first item, called the head (head in code).
  • Each node has two parts:
    • Data: the value the node carries (a primitive or an object).
    • Link (pointer): a reference to the next node; null in the last node.

Basics

Where Do Nodes Live in Memory?

  • Items are not stored contiguously; each node is created separately with new.
  • Still, the list is a linear structure: every node except the last has exactly one successor.
  • The order comes from the references in the next fields, not from memory addresses.

The list order is 10 → 1 → 8 → 11, but the nodes sit in memory in a different order; the arrows follow the references.

Basics

The Node Class

int data 
// Node class
class Node {
    int data;
    Node next;
    Node(int data) {
        this.data = data;
        this.next = null;
    }
}
Generic version 
// Node class
class Node<T> {
    T data;
    Node<T> next;
    Node(T data) {
        this.data = data;
        this.next = null;
    }
}
  • The class has a field of its own type (Node next): a self-referential structure.
  • The generic version stores any type: Node<String> d = new Node<>("Ann");
  • A new node's next field starts as null and changes once the node is linked into a list.

Building a Singly Linked List

new Node(10): creates a node with data = 10 and next = null; first points to it.

The second node (1) is created. The nodes are not linked yet.

The third node (8) is created. Each node can sit anywhere in memory.

The fourth node (11) is created. We have four separate nodes, each with a next field of null (⁄).

first.next = second: the next field of 10 now points to 1 (orange).

second.next = third: links 1 → 8.

third.next = fourth: the list is ready: 10 → 1 → 8 → 11 → null. first alone is enough to reach the whole list.

Basics

Singly Linked List Operations

OperationHow it worksCost
Insert at headNew node points to the old head; head becomes the new nodeO(1)
Insert at tailWalk to the last node (no walk with a tail pointer)O(n) · O(1)
Delete at headMove head to the next nodeO(1)
Delete at tailMust find the second-to-last nodeO(n)
Search · print · lengthWalk from head to tailO(n)
Reverse · mergeOne pass over the lists (merge needs a tail pointer)O(n)

n: number of nodes. Reaching the i-th item is also O(n): unlike an array, we cannot jump to an index.

public class SinglyLinkedList {
    private Node head = null, tail = null;
    private int size = 0;    // number of items
    public int size() { return size; }
    public boolean isEmpty() { return size == 0; }
    public Integer first() {
        return isEmpty() ? null : head.data; }

}

Basics

Singly Linked Lists: Pros and Cons

Advantages

  • Easy to implement.
  • Insert / delete at the head in O(1); inserting in the middle needs no shifting.
  • Dynamic size: no capacity reserved in advance; the item count can change freely.

Disadvantages

  • Search is slow: O(n).
  • No random access; reaching the i-th item means walking from the head.
  • Each node carries an extra reference (more memory).
  • Cannot be traversed backward.
Inserting or deleting in the middle is O(1) only if we already know the position (the previous node); finding it still takes an O(n) walk.

Traversing and Printing a List

temp = head: the walk starts at the head. head never changes; only temp moves.

Print the heading.

temp != null (node 10) → enter the loop body.

temp = temp.next → temp is now node(1).

temp = node(1) ≠ null → continue.

Print temp.data = 1.

temp = temp.next → temp is now node(8).

Print temp.data = 8.

temp == null → the condition is false and the loop ends.

Print null at the end. For n nodes the loop runs n times: O(n).

void printList() {
    Node temp = head;
    System.out.print("Linked List: ");
    while (temp != null) {
        System.out.print(temp.data + " -> ");
        temp = temp.next;
    }
    System.out.println("null");
}

Singly Linked: Traversal and Insertion

Same Pattern: Length and Search

O(n) 
int listLength() {
    int length = 0;
    Node temp = head;
    while (temp != null) {
        length++;
        temp = temp.next;
    }
    return length;
}
O(n) 
int search(int target) {
    Node temp = head;
    int position = 0;
    while (temp != null) {
        if (temp.data == target)
            return position;
        position++;
        temp = temp.next;
    }
    return -1;   // not found
}
The traversal pattern: start with temp = head, do the work while temp != null, and advance with temp = temp.next. If the length is needed often, keep a size field and update it on every insertion and deletion; the length then costs O(1).

10 == 8? No → continue.

position++ → 1.

position++ → 2.

temp = temp.next → node(8).

temp = node(8) ≠ null → loop.

8 == 8 → found the target.

return 2. We looked at 3 nodes; in the worst case (target absent) we look at all n: O(n), result −1.

Inserting at the Head — O(1)

Call addFirst(11). The list is empty: head = null.

Create node 11; its next is null.

newNode.next = head: head is null, so 11's next stays null.

head = newNode: head moves to 11: 11 → null.

if (tail == null) tail = head: the list was empty, so 11 is both head and tail. size++ → 1.

Call addFirst(8). List: 11 → null.

Create node 8; its next is null.

newNode.next = head: 8 points to the old head (11). Changing head first would lose 11.

head = newNode: head moves to 8: 8 → 11 → null.

tail is not null, so it stays at 11. size++ → 2.

Call addFirst(1). List: 8 → 11 → null.

Create node 1; its next is null.

newNode.next = head: 1 points to the old head (8). Changing head first would lose 8.

head = newNode: head moves to 1: 1 → 8 → 11 → null.

tail stays at 11. size++ → 3. However long the list, a fixed number of assignments: O(1).

void addFirst(int data) {
    Node newNode = new Node(data);
    newNode.next = head;
    head = newNode;
    if (tail == null) tail = head;
    size++;
}

Inserting at the Tail — O(n)

addLast(10): create the new node.

head == null → the list is empty.

head = newNode: a one-node list.

return: no walk needed.

addLast(1): create the new node.

The list is not empty → walk to the end.

temp = head: start at the head to find the last node.

node(10).next == null → temp is at the last node; the loop ends.

temp.next = newNode: 10 → 1 → null.

addLast(8): create the new node.

The list is not empty → walk to the end.

temp = head: start at the head to find the last node.

node(10).next is not null → advance.

temp = temp.next → node(1).

node(1).next == null → temp is at the last node; the loop ends.

temp.next = newNode: 10 → 1 → 8 → null. Every insertion walks to the end: O(n).

void addLast(int data) {
    Node newNode = new Node(data);
    if (head == null) {
        head = newNode;
        return;
    }
    Node temp = head;
    while (temp.next != null)
        temp = temp.next;
    temp.next = newNode;
}

Singly Linked: Traversal and Insertion

Inserting at the Tail with a Tail Pointer — O(1)

class SinglyLinkedList {
    Node head, tail;  int size;
    void addLast(int data) {
        Node newNode = new Node(data);
        if (head == null) {
            head = tail = newNode;
        } else {
            tail.next = newNode;
            tail = newNode;
        }
        size++;
    }
}
No walk: O(1)The last node is known; two assignments suffice.
The priceEvery operation must keep tail up to date (inserting into an empty list, deleting the last node).
Deleting at the tail is still O(n)In a singly linked list we cannot step back from tail.

The list is not empty; the last node is already known: node(1).

Singly Linked: Traversal and Insertion

Inserting at a Given Position

void addAt(int data, int index) {   // index starts at 0
    if (index == 0) { addFirst(data); return; }
    Node temp = head;
    for (int i = 0; i < index - 1 && temp != null; i++)
        temp = temp.next;
    if (temp == null) {          // list shorter than index
        System.out.println("Position not found.");
        return;
    }
    Node newNode = new Node(data);
    newNode.next = temp.next;           // (1)
    temp.next = newNode;                // (2)
    if (temp == tail) tail = newNode;   // inserted at the end
    size++;
}
Index 0Same as inserting at the head; handled separately.
Order mattersFirst (1), then (2); the reverse cuts off the rest of the list.
CostWalking to the position is O(index), O(n) in the worst case; linking is O(1).

(1) newNode.next = temp.next: 5 points to 8. The list has not changed yet.

(2) temp.next = newNode: 10 → 1 → 5 → 8 → 11. Only 2 links changed; in the reverse order the path to 8 would be lost.

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations · Step through the code

Deleting at the Head — O(1)

Call 1: head is not null (10 → 1 → 11 → null).

temp = head: save the node being removed (10).

head = head.next: head is node(1); 10 is now unreachable.

temp.next = null: 10 is fully detached.

return temp: 10 goes back to the caller. Once unreferenced, it is reclaimed by the GC. O(1).

Call 2: head is not null (1 → 11 → null).

temp = head: save the node being removed (1).

head = head.next: head is node(11); 1 is now unreachable.

temp.next = null: 1 is fully detached.

return temp: 1 goes back to the caller. Once unreferenced, it is reclaimed by the GC. O(1).

Call 3: head is not null (11 → null).

temp = head: save the node being removed (11).

head = head.next: head is null and the list is empty; 11 is now unreachable.

temp.next = null: 11 is fully detached.

return temp: 11 goes back to the caller. Once unreferenced, it is reclaimed by the GC. O(1).

On an empty list, head == null → return null. Without this check, head.next would throw a NullPointerException.

Node removeFirst() {
    if (head == null)
        return null;
    Node temp = head;
    head = head.next;  if (head == null) tail = null;
    temp.next = null;  size--;
    return temp;
}

Deleting at the Tail — O(n)

The list is not empty.

head.next is not null → there is more than one node.

temp = head. Goal: find the second-to-last node (its link will change).

node(10).next.next = 8 ≠ null → advance.

temp = temp.next → node(1).

node(1).next.next = 11 ≠ null → advance.

temp = temp.next → node(8).

node(8).next.next == null → temp is at the second-to-last node.

temp.next = null: 11 leaves the list → 10 → 1 → 8 → null. O(n); a tail pointer doesn't help, because we cannot step back.

void removeLast() {
    if (head == null) return;
    if (head.next == null) {  // single node
        head = tail = null;  size--;
        return;
    }
    Node temp = head;
    while (temp.next.next != null)
        temp = temp.next;
    temp.next = null;  tail = temp;  size--;
}

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations

Deleting a Given Item

void remove(int key) {
    if (head == null) return;
    if (head.data == key) {
        head = head.next;  size--;
        if (head == null) tail = null;  return;
    }
    Node prev = head;
    Node temp = head.next;
    while (temp != null) {
        if (temp.data == key) {
            prev.next = temp.next;
            if (temp == tail) tail = prev;  size--;
            return;
        }
        prev = temp;
        temp = temp.next;
    }
    System.out.println("Not found.");
}

prev.next = temp.next
the doomed node is "skipped"

  • Two pointers walk together: deleting needs the previous node.
  • Deleting the head is a separate case.
  • Search O(n) + relinking O(1) → O(n).

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations

Reversing a List

void reverse() {
    tail = head;                 // old head becomes the new tail
    Node prev = null;
    Node current = head;
    Node next = null;
    while (current != null) {
        next = current.next;  // 1) save next
        current.next = prev;  // 2) reverse the link
        prev = current;       // 3) advance prev
        current = next;       // 4) advance current
    }
    head = prev;
}
Three pointersprev, current, next
No new nodesEach round reverses one link.
O(n) timeO(1) extra space

Code Trace: reverse()

Start: prev = null, current = head (10), next = null. No new nodes will be created.

Round 1: current = node(10) is not null.

1) next = current.next = node(8): so the rest of the list survives the cut.

2) current.next = prev: 10 now points to null (link reversed).

3–4) prev = current; current = next: both pointers move one node forward.

Round 2: current = node(8) is not null.

1) next = current.next = node(1): so the rest of the list survives the cut.

2) current.next = prev: 8 now points to node(10) (link reversed).

3–4) prev = current; current = next: both pointers move one node forward.

Round 3: current = node(1) is not null.

1) next = current.next = node(11): so the rest of the list survives the cut.

2) current.next = prev: 1 now points to node(8) (link reversed).

3–4) prev = current; current = next: both pointers move one node forward.

Round 4: current = node(11) is not null.

1) next = current.next = null: so the rest of the list survives the cut.

2) current.next = prev: 11 now points to node(1) (link reversed).

3–4) prev = current; current = next: both pointers move one node forward.

current == null → the loop ends; prev is at the old last node (11).

head = prev: the new list is 11 → 1 → 8 → 10 → null. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations · Step through the code

Finding the Middle: Slow and Fast Pointers

The list is not empty (an empty list throws an exception).

Both pointers start at the head. We find the middle without knowing the length.

fast = node(10) and fast.next = node(8) are not null → round 1.

slow moves 1 step → node(8).

fast moves 2 steps → node(1).

fast = node(1) and fast.next = node(11) are not null → round 2.

slow moves 1 step → node(1).

fast moves 2 steps → node(5).

fast.next == null → fast has reached the end; the loop ends. In 2 rounds slow took 2 steps and fast took 4.

return 1: the slow pointer is in the middle. One pass, O(n). For an even length it returns the second middle (10, 8, 1, 11 → 1).

int findMiddle() {
    if (head == null)
        throw new IllegalStateException("List is empty");
    Node slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;       // 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next;  // 2 steps
    }
    return slow.data;
}

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations

Copying a List

SinglyLinkedList copy() {
    SinglyLinkedList newList =
        new SinglyLinkedList();
    Node temp = head;
    while (temp != null) {
        newList.addLast(temp.data);
        temp = temp.next;
    }
    return newList;
}
Deep copyNew nodes are created; writing newList.head = head would only give a second reference to the same list.
CostIf addLast walks to the end every time, the total is O(n²); with a tail pointer, O(n).

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations

Removing Duplicates from a List

void removeDuplicates() {
    SinglyLinkedList seen =
        new SinglyLinkedList();
    Node prev = null, temp = head;
    while (temp != null) {
        int v = temp.data;
        if (seen.contains(v)) {
            prev.next =
                temp.next;   // skip
            if (temp == tail) tail = prev;  size--;
        } else {
            seen.addFirst(v);
            prev = temp;
        }
        temp = temp.next;
    }
}
IdeaKeep the values seen so far in a second list; skip any node that repeats one.
CostA search in the seen list for every node: O(n²). With a hash set, O(n).
NoteThe first node is never a duplicate, so no deletion happens while prev is null.

contains(v): search(v) != -1. Example: 3 → 5 → 3 → 7 → 5 ⇒ 3 → 5 → 7

Singly Linked: Deletion and Other Operations

Merging Two Sorted Lists

SinglyLinkedList merge(
        SinglyLinkedList l1,
        SinglyLinkedList l2) {
    SinglyLinkedList result =
        new SinglyLinkedList();
    Node p1 = l1.head, p2 = l2.head;
    while (p1 != null && p2 != null) {
        if (p1.data <= p2.data) {
            result.addLast(p1.data);
            p1 = p1.next;
        } else {
            result.addLast(p2.data);
            p2 = p2.next;
        }
    }
    // append the leftovers
    while (p1 != null) {
        result.addLast(p1.data);
        p1 = p1.next;
    }
    while (p2 != null) {
        result.addLast(p2.data);
        p2 = p2.next;
    }
    return result;
}
1 → 4 → 7 and 2 → 3 → 8
⇒ 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 7 → 8

If addLast is O(1) (tail pointer), the total is O(n + m) (n, m: list lengths); if each insertion walks to the end, O((n + m)²).

Sorting a Singly Linked List

void sort() {
    Node current = head;
    while (current != null) {
        Node other = current.next;
        while (other != null) {
            if (current.data > other.data) {
                int temp = current.data;
                current.data = other.data;
                other.data = temp;
            }
            other = other.next;
        }
        current = current.next;
    }
}
Swap valuesThe nodes stay in place; only their data fields change.
O(n²)Each node is compared with every node after it: n(n−1)/2.
BetterMerge sort runs in O(n log n) on a linked list and needs no extra array.

4 > 1 → swap the values (temp = 4). List: 1 → 4 → 3 → 2.

1 > 3? No → no swap; other advances.

1 > 2? No → no swap; other advances.

The inner loop is done: the smallest remaining value is now in current's node. current advances → node(4).

void sort() {
    Node current = head;
    while (current != null) {
        Node other = current.next;
        while (other != null) {
            if (current.data > other.data) {
                int temp = current.data;
                current.data = other.data;
                other.data = temp;
            }
            other = other.next;
        }
        current = current.next;
    }
}

Doubly Linked List

Doubly Linked List

  • A structure whose nodes are linked in both directions.
  • Each node holds two pointers: one to the previous node and one to the next.
  • The list can be walked either way; usually both a head (head) and a tail (tail) are kept.
GainBackward traversal; deleting a known node or the last node in O(1).
PriceA second reference per node; every insertion and deletion must update both directions.

Doubly Linked List

Doubly Linked List: Node and Structure

class Node {
    int data;
    Node prev;
    Node next;
    Node(int data) {
        this.data = data;
        this.prev = null;
        this.next = null;
    }
}
  • Items can be reached going forward or backward.
  • Inserting a node means updating pointers in both directions.
  • Removing a node means updating the pointers of both the previous and the next node.
  • A search can walk forward or backward.
  • The list keeps the fields Node head, tail;.

Doubly Linked List · Step through the code

Inserting at the Head of a Doubly Linked List — O(1)

addFirst(1): the new node's prev and next fields are null (⁄).

head is not null → else branch.

newNode.next = head: forward link 1 → 10.

head.prev = newNode: backward link 10 → 1 (10's null is gone).

head = newNode: 1 ⇄ 10 ⇄ 15 ⇄ 25. O(1). Had the list been empty, head and tail would both become the new node.

public void addFirst(int data) {
    Node newNode = new Node(data);
    if (head == null) {
        head = newNode;
        tail = newNode;
    } else {
        newNode.next = head;
        head.prev = newNode;
        head = newNode;
    }
}

Doubly Linked List · Step through the code

Inserting at the Tail of a Doubly Linked List — O(1)

addLast(30): create the new node.

The list is not empty → else. tail gives the last node directly.

newNode.prev = tail: backward link 30 → 25.

tail.next = newNode: forward link 25 → 30.

tail = newNode: 1 ⇄ 10 ⇄ 15 ⇄ 25 ⇄ 30. No walk: O(1).

public void addLast(int data) {
    Node newNode = new Node(data);
    if (head == null) {
        head = newNode;
        tail = newNode;
    } else {
        newNode.prev = tail;
        tail.next = newNode;
        tail = newNode;
    }
}

Doubly Linked List

Inserting at a Position in a Doubly Linked List

void addAt(int data, int index) {   // index starts at 0
    if (index == 0) { addFirst(data); return; }
    Node temp = head;
    for (int i = 0; i < index - 1 && temp != null; i++)
        temp = temp.next;
    if (temp == null) { System.out.println("Invalid position."); return; }
    if (temp == tail) { addLast(data); return; }   // updates tail too
    Node newNode = new Node(data);
    newNode.next = temp.next;     // (1)
    newNode.prev = temp;          // (2)
    temp.next.prev = newNode;     // (3)
    temp.next = newNode;          // (4)
}

Code Trace: addAt(12, 2) — the linking part

addAt(12, 2): as in the singly linked version, temp has walked to the node at index − 1 = 1 (10). Create the new node.

(1) newNode.next = temp.next: 12 → 15. The list has not changed yet.

(2) newNode.prev = temp: backward link 12 → 10.

(3) temp.next.prev = newNode: 15's backward link now points to 12. This must come before (4), while temp.next is still 15.

(4) temp.next = newNode: 10 → 12. Four links changed; swapping (3) and (4) would leave 15 unreachable.

Result (drawing tidied): 1 ⇄ 10 ⇄ 12 ⇄ 15 ⇄ 25. Linking is O(1); walking to the position is O(n).

Doubly Linked List

Deleting a Given Item from a Doubly Linked List

void remove(int data) {
    Node temp = head;
    while (temp != null && temp.data != data)
        temp = temp.next;
    if (temp == null) return;  // not found
    if (temp.prev != null)
        temp.prev.next = temp.next;
    else head = temp.next;   // removing the head
    if (temp.next != null)
        temp.next.prev = temp.prev;
    else tail = temp.prev;    // removing the tail
}

The removed node's neighbors are linked to each other. If the head or the tail is removed, update head/tail. Search O(n), deletion O(1).

void printBackward() {
    Node temp = tail;
    System.out.print("Backward: ");
    while (temp != null) {
        System.out.print(temp.data + " <-> ");
        temp = temp.prev;
    }
    System.out.println("null");
}

Doubly Linked List

Sentinel Nodes: Header and Trailer

IdeaPut two fixed nodes that carry no data at the ends of the list (Goodrich–Tamassia: header / trailer).
No special casesEvery real node always has a predecessor and a successor: no null checks, no head/tail updates.
PriceTwo extra nodes; traversal starts at header.next and stops at trailer.

Doubly Linked List · Step through the code

Code Trace: Inserting and Deleting with Sentinels

Empty list: just the two sentinels, pointing to each other. size = 0. Only the sentinels' outer ends are null.

addFirst(10): addBetween(10, header, header.next). In an empty list, header.next is the trailer.

new Node(10): a new node with both links null.

newNode.prev = pred → node(—).

newNode.next = succ → node(—). The new node is ready; the list doesn't see it yet.

pred.next = newNode: forward — → 10.

succ.prev = newNode: now linked backward too; size = 1. No if: pred and succ always exist.

addFirst(5): addBetween(5, header, header.next) — 5 goes between the header and 10. Same code, no special case.

new Node(5): a new node with both links null.

newNode.prev = pred → node(—).

newNode.next = succ → node(10). The new node is ready; the list doesn't see it yet.

pred.next = newNode: forward — → 5.

succ.prev = newNode: now linked backward too; size = 2. No if: pred and succ always exist.

remove(d), d = node(10) (the last real node). Thanks to the sentinels, both neighbors are guaranteed to exist.

d.prev.next = d.next: 5 now points straight to the trailer.

d.next.prev = d.prev: 10 is skipped in both directions; size = 1. Even when the last node goes, there is no tail update → every operation is O(1).

void addBetween(int v, Node pred, Node succ) {
    Node newNode = new Node(v);
    newNode.prev = pred;
    newNode.next = succ;
    pred.next = newNode;
    succ.prev = newNode;  size++;
}
void addFirst(int v) {
    addBetween(v, header, header.next); }
void remove(Node d) {
    d.prev.next = d.next;
    d.next.prev = d.prev;
    size--; }

Doubly Linked List

Multi-Way Links: Turning a Matrix into a Linked Structure

Each node holds two links: class Node { int data; Node right, down; } (constructor: Node(int data))

void display(Node start) {
    Node down = start;
    while (down != null) {       // rows
        Node right = down;
        while (right != null) {     // columns
            System.out.print(right.data + " ");
            right = right.right;
        }
        System.out.println();
        down = down.down;
    }
}

Output, row by row: 1 2 3 / 4 5 6 / 7 8 9. Each node is visited once: O(rows · columns).

Doubly Linked List

Building the Linked Structure from a Matrix

Node build(int[][] m) {
    int r = m.length, c = m[0].length;
    Node[][] d = new Node[r][c];
    for (int i = r - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        for (int j = c - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
            Node n = new Node(m[i][j]);
            if (j + 1 < c) n.right = d[i][j+1];
            if (i + 1 < r) n.down = d[i+1][j];
            d[i][j] = n;
        }
    return d[0][0];
}
Start at the bottom rightThe right and lower neighbors already exist; each cell gets one node.
O(rows · columns)Each cell is processed once.
Why the d table? A recursive version that calls build(i, j+1) and build(i+1, j) directly rebuilds the same cell over and over (an exponential number of nodes; the right and down paths don't share a common node).

Doubly Linked List · Step through the code

Code Trace: build(m) — a 2×3 matrix

d: a 2×3 array of node references, all null. Nodes will be created starting from the bottom right.

(i=1, j=2): new Node(6); no right (last column), no down (last row). Neighbors already exist; no cell is built twice.

(i=1, j=1): new Node(5); right → 6, no down (last row). Neighbors already exist; no cell is built twice.

(i=1, j=0): new Node(4); right → 5, no down (last row). Neighbors already exist; no cell is built twice.

(i=0, j=2): new Node(3); no right (last column), down → 6. Neighbors already exist; no cell is built twice.

(i=0, j=1): new Node(2); right → 3, down → 5. Neighbors already exist; no cell is built twice.

(i=0, j=0): new Node(1); right → 2, down → 4. Neighbors already exist; no cell is built twice.

Return d[0][0] (1): the whole structure is reachable from the top-left corner through right/down. 6 cells, 6 nodes → O(r·c).

Node build(int[][] m) {
    int r = m.length, c = m[0].length;
    Node[][] d = new Node[r][c];
    for (int i = r - 1; i >= 0; i--)
        for (int j = c - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
            Node n = new Node(m[i][j]);
            if (j + 1 < c) n.right = d[i][j+1];
            if (i + 1 < r) n.down = d[i+1][j];
            d[i][j] = n;
        }
    return d[0][0];
}

Circularly Linked List

Circularly Linked List

  • The last node points to the first node instead of null, so the list forms a cycle (a ring).
  • Each node still points to the node after it; the list has no null links.
  • Keeping tail alone is enough: the head is tail.next.
  • Uses: jobs that take turns (round-robin scheduling), turn order in multiplayer games, a looping playlist.

Circularly Linked List

The Circular List Class

public class CircularLinkedList {
    class Node {
        int data;
        Node next;
        Node(int data) {
            this.data = data;
            this.next = null;
        }
    }
    private Node tail;  // head = tail.next
    private int size;
}
Why only tail?Head = tail.next, so both ends are reachable in O(1).
Keeping head as wellEvery operation would have to update two pointers; unnecessary.
Special casesEmpty: tail == null. One node: tail.next == tail.

Circularly Linked List · Step through the code

Printing a Circular List

The list is not empty. Only tail is kept; the last node points to the head (the bottom link).

The head is tail.next: current = 1.

current (1) != tail (16) → loop.

Print 1.

current = current.next → node(8).

current (8) != tail (16) → loop.

Print 8.

current = current.next → node(10).

current (10) != tail (16) → loop.

Print 10.

current = current.next → node(16).

current == tail → the loop ends (we never reach null; the condition is != tail).

The last node is printed separately after the loop. Each node once: O(n).

void print() {
    if (tail == null) return;
    Node current = tail.next;
    while (current != tail) {
        System.out.print(current.data + " ");
        current = current.next;
    }
    System.out.print(current.data + " ");
}

Circularly Linked List

Detecting a Cycle in General: Floyd's Algorithm

boolean hasCycle(Node head) {
    Node slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null &&
           fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}
  • Each round, the slow pointer moves one node and the fast pointer two.
  • If there is a cycle, the two pointers eventually meet inside it.
  • If there is no cycle, the fast pointer reaches null.
  • The cycle need not lead back to the head node.
TimeO(n)
Extra spaceO(1)
Following the nodes until we get back to head is not enough: the cycle may loop back to a node in the middle of the list.

Circularly Linked List · Step through the code

Code Trace: hasCycle (Floyd)

The list is 1 → … → 6, and 6 points back to 3 (the cycle does not return to the head). Both pointers start at the head.

Round 1: fast (1) and fast.next (2) are not null.

slow moves 1 step → node(2).

fast moves 2 steps → node(3).

slow (2) ≠ fast (3) → continue.

Round 2: fast (3) and fast.next (4) are not null.

slow moves 1 step → node(3).

fast moves 2 steps → node(5).

slow (3) ≠ fast (5) → continue.

Round 3: fast (5) and fast.next (6) are not null.

slow moves 1 step → node(4).

fast moves 2 steps → node(3).

slow (4) ≠ fast (3) → continue. fast has entered the cycle and is closing in on slow from behind.

Round 4: fast (3) and fast.next (4) are not null.

slow moves 1 step → node(5).

fast moves 2 steps → node(5).

slow == fast (node 5) → return true. Inside the cycle, fast gains one node on slow each round; O(n) time, O(1) space.

boolean hasCycle(Node head) {
    Node slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null &&
           fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Inserting and Deleting at the Head of a Circular List

O(1) 
void addFirst(int value) {
    Node temp = new Node(value);
    if (tail == null) {
        tail = temp;
        tail.next = tail;
    } else {
        temp.next = tail.next;
        tail.next = temp;
    }   // tail unchanged
    size++;
}
O(1) 
void removeFirst() {
    if (tail == null) return;
    Node head = tail.next;
    if (head == tail)   // single node
        tail = null;
    else
        tail.next = head.next;
    size--;
}
Inserting at the head is inserting at the tail minus the line tail = temp: the new node enters the ring at the same spot; only which node counts as the "tail" changes.

Circularly Linked List

Deleting at the Tail of a Circular List — O(n)

void removeLast() {
    if (tail == null) return;
    if (tail.next == tail) tail = null;   // single node
    else {
        Node temp = tail.next;
        while (temp.next != tail)     // second to last
            temp = temp.next;
        temp.next = tail.next;     // link to the head
        tail = temp;
    }
    size--;
}

Finding the second-to-last node means walking around the ring: O(n). In a doubly linked circular list, tail.prev makes it O(1).

temp = temp.next → node(10).

node(10).next == tail → temp is at the second-to-last node.

temp.next = tail.next: 10 points to the head (1); 16 has left the ring.

tail = temp: tail is now 10.

size--. Ring: 1 → 8 → 10 → (1). We walked to find the previous node: O(n).

if (tail == null) return;
if (tail.next == tail) tail = null;   // single node
else {
    Node temp = tail.next;
    while (temp.next != tail)  // second to last
        temp = temp.next;
    temp.next = tail.next;  // link to the head
    tail = temp;
}
size--;

Circularly Linked List · Step through the code

Code Trace: Round-Robin with rotate()

Ring 1 → 8 → 10 → (1), tail = 10, head = tail.next = 1. Three jobs take turns on the processor.

Round 1: the job at the head, 1, is served (printed).

rotate(): tail = tail.next → tail = 1. No link changes, one pointer moves: O(1). New head: 8.

Round 2: the job at the head, 8, is served (printed).

rotate(): tail = tail.next → tail = 8. No link changes, one pointer moves: O(1). New head: 10.

Round 3: the job at the head, 10, is served (printed).

rotate(): tail = tail.next → tail = 10. No link changes, one pointer moves: O(1). New head: 1.

Round 4: the job at the head, 1, is served (printed).

rotate(): tail = tail.next → tail = 1. No link changes, one pointer moves: O(1). Output 1 8 10 1: the jobs take fair turns.

void rotate() {              // Goodrich: rotate()
    if (tail != null)
        tail = tail.next;   // old head becomes the tail
}
// round-robin: serve the head each round
for (int round = 1; round <= 4; round++) {
    System.out.print(tail.next.data + " ");
    list.rotate();
}

Summary

Array or Linked List?

CriterionArrayLinked list
Access the i-th itemO(1): compute the addressO(n): walk from the head
Insert / delete at the frontO(n): shiftingO(1)
Insert after a known positionO(n)O(1): two links
Sizefixed; growing costs an O(n) copydynamic; one new per insertion
Overhead / cacheunused capacity; cache-friendlya reference per node; scattered access

Frequent random access and a fixed size → array. Frequent insertion/deletion at the ends and an unpredictable size → linked list (stack, queue).

Summary

Common Mistakes with Linked Lists

No empty-list checkhead.data while head is null → NullPointerException.if (head == null) return;
Linking in the wrong orderIf head changes first, the old list is lost.newNode.next = head; head = newNode;
Advancing head during a traversalAfter printing, the list is unreachable.Node temp = head;
Forgetting tailAfter the only node is deleted, tail still points to it.if (head == null) tail = null;
One direction in a doubly linked listIf prev isn't updated, backward traversal breaks.next.prev = newNode;
!= null in a circular listA ring has no null → infinite loop.while (p != tail) …

Summary

Operation Costs Across Linked Lists

OperationSingly
(head only)		Singly
(head + tail)		Doubly
(head + tail)		Circular
(tail only)
Insert at headO(1)O(1)O(1)O(1)
Insert at tailO(n)O(1)O(1)O(1)
Delete at headO(1)O(1)O(1)O(1)
Delete at tailO(n)O(n)O(1)O(n)
Search / i-th itemO(n)O(n)O(n)O(n)
Delete a known nodeO(n)*O(n)*O(1)O(n)*

* Finding the previous node takes a walk. Inserting after a known node is O(1) in every kind. In an array, by contrast, reaching the i-th item is O(1) and inserting at the front O(n).

Summary

Sample Problems

  1. What does it take to make inserting at the tail of a singly linked list O(1)? Which operation is still O(n)?
  2. What happens if the two lines of addFirst are swapped (head = newNode; first)?
  3. How do you find the middle of a list in one pass, without computing its length?
  4. How can you tell whether a singly linked list has a cycle (the last node linked back to an earlier one)?
  5. What does it cost to delete the tail node of a doubly linked list? Why is it different for a singly linked list?
  6. Why does a circular list keep tail rather than head?
Show answers
  1. A tail pointer. Deleting at the tail stays O(n) (we cannot step back to the previous node).
  2. The new node points to itself (newNode.next = newNode) and the old list is lost.
  3. Slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) pointers: when fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle.
  4. The same two pointers (Floyd): if fast reaches null there is no cycle; if it catches up with slow, there is one.
  5. O(1): tail = tail.prev. In a singly linked list, reaching the previous node means walking from the head: O(n).
  6. Head = tail.next; one pointer gives O(1) access to both ends.

Summary

Exercises

  1. In the list 3 → 5 → 7, what is the list after head.next = head.next.next;? What happens to 5?
  2. What does int mystery(Node d) { return d == null ? 0 : d.data + mystery(d.next); } return for 2 → 4 → 6?
  3. How do you find the k-th item from the end of a singly linked list in one pass, without knowing its length?
  4. In a doubly linked list with sentinels, how many link assignments does inserting into an empty list take? Why is no if needed?
  5. Circular list 1 → 8 → 10 (tail = 10). After two calls to rotate(), which item is at the head?
  6. How many comparisons and swaps does sort() make on the list 3 → 1 → 2?
Answers / hints
  1. 3 → 7; if no reference to 5 remains, the garbage collector reclaims it.
  2. 12: a recursive sum; O(n) time, O(n) call stack.
  3. Two pointers: fast goes k steps ahead, then both move together; when fast is null, slow is the answer.
  4. 4 (newNode.prev, newNode.next, pred.next, succ.prev); the sentinel neighbors always exist.
  5. 10 (tail moves to 1, then to 8; head = tail.next).
  6. 3 comparisons, 2 swaps → 1 → 2 → 3.
